title: Control Time Model: Wait One Second and Start Your Journey

source_quality.notes: Complete UTF-8 page extraction plus bounded contact and focused formula/table/plot review.

task_reconstruction.summary: Design a toll-plaza merging area that balances capacity, safety, geometry, booth technology, and cost under changing vehicle and service conditions.

section_map.summary: Input: Daily congestion, long commutes, and the post-toll merge motivate a plaza design problem. Rhetorical job: Route the reader through assumptions, baseline diagnosis, CTM/WAM construction, comparison, modifications, sensitivity, and closure. Analytical job: Keep each promised stage attached to its later metric and avoid treating the route itself as evidence. Output: A six-paragraph research-flow abstract that selects CTM in general and announces later reliability checks. Handoff: The authority letter converts that pipeline into operational advice and worked values.

Input: The New Jersey Turnpike Authority needs a safer and more orderly post-toll merge. Rhetorical job: Diagnose the current plaza, introduce CTM in plain language, report headline efficiency/risk/cost claims, and recommend future construction consideration. Analytical job: Translate model outputs into an audience decision while preserving the difference between simulation, theory, expectation, and recommendation. Output: A direct recommendation built around one-second-safe release spacing and a claimed all-aspect advantage. Handoff: The numbered introduction restates the design task, metrics, and external conditions more formally.

Input: Highways require costly infrastructure, toll plazas create merge constraints, and the prompt requests shape, size, pattern, comparison, and adaptation. Rhetorical job: Move from public relevance to a typed task and then use literature to accept or reject design principles. Analytical job: Identify B and L, three evaluation axes, autonomous/payment extensions, and the barrier and lane-placement choices inherited from prior work. Output: A three-paragraph chain: three-objective context -> formal deliverables -> literature-based design decisions. Handoff: The assumptions convert those deliverables into tractable motion, arrival, and service premises.

Input: The real plaza includes heterogeneous behavior, arrivals, acceleration, queues, service times, and vehicle dimensions. Rhetorical job: List one simplification at a time and usually pair it with a practical reason. Analytical job: Fix rational lane following, heavy-traffic arrival spacing, simple kinematics, stopped queues, normal human-booth service, and negligible vehicle length. Output: A conditional operating regime in which the release and merge recurrences can be written. Handoff: The notation table assigns symbols and units to the retained quantities.

Input: The task and assumptions use lane, booth, distance, radius, time, speed, and acceleration quantities. Rhetorical job: Create a compact symbol interface before model construction. Analytical job: Define L, B, D, d_l, d_b, r, T_h, t_0, v_m, a_s, and a_b with roles and units. Output: A reusable symbol table feeding kinematics, geometry, throughput, risk, and cost. Handoff: The Models overview consumes the notation to compare EM, CTM, and WAM.

Input: Existing plazas either allow free post-toll merging or assign predefined merge points. Rhetorical job: Give each baseline a fair light-traffic reading before exposing its heavy-traffic failure. Analytical job: Distinguish unpredictability, simultaneous arrival conflict, braking, blockage, and throughput consequences. Output: A diagnosed baseline whose failures motivate a release-time controller rather than only new lane markings. Handoff: Section 4.2 introduces CTM as the direct response to those failures.

Input: The baseline fails because vehicles assigned to one downstream lane may leave neighboring booths too close together. Rhetorical job: Present CTM as an orderly, safer alternative and make the one-second rule, geometry, mapping, and design optimization inspectable. Analytical job: Derive a residual braking time, set t0, simulate throughput, define f and i_k, bound D, and balance booth groups across lanes. Output: A control rule plus a two-arc merge geometry and near-even booth-to-lane allocation; for B=8,L=3, D=105.5 m and three optimal patterns are reported. Handoff: WAM asks whether separating service completion from physical release can recover the waiting time CTM introduces.

Input: CTM can keep a serviced vehicle at the booth while it waits for the safe release time. Rhetorical job: Treat that occupation as a specific CTM inefficiency and propose a waiting-area variant without claiming it will win. Analytical job: Decouple service completion from release, allow the following vehicle to enter service, and defer comparison to throughput analysis. Output: A competing CTM variant with a waiting buffer and an explicit later evaluation promise. Handoff: Section 5.1 derives parallel recurrences and decides whether the added land is justified.

Input: EM, CTM, and WAM need a common hourly efficiency measure under manual-booth, two-to-one, heavy-traffic conditions. Rhetorical job: Define throughput, derive one recurrence per candidate, simulate them in parallel, and use a test plus practical cost to select among them. Analytical job: Model manual service as N(15,4), add PET delay for EM, impose controlled release recurrences for CTM/WAM, stop at one hour, and compare distributions. Output: A reported near-tie between EM and CTM, a roughly 1.6 veh/h WAM gain, and a decision to discard WAM because the land cost outweighs the gain. Handoff: The paper retains CTM and moves to PET-based accident prevention.

Input: CTM has survived the throughput screen but must be compared with EM on conflict risk. Rhetorical job: Make safety legible through PET, a probability proxy, simulated distributions, and an accident-rate table. Analytical job: Define PET severity, posit p=exp(-PET)/100, simulate EM/CTM PET, and convert event probabilities to accidents per 100,000 vehicles. Output: A claimed 13.66% CTM reduction and one-second PET floor, accompanied by a Table 2 label/value conflict preserved for G7. Handoff: The next section estimates land, booth, and operating cost for the retained design.

Input: The retained plaza requires land, booth construction, and annual human/automatic operation resources. Rhetorical job: Convert geometry and booth types into fixed and annual cost quantities with one worked example. Analytical job: Use symmetric outer boundaries to estimate area, multiply by land price, add booth construction, and sum annual booth operating terms. Output: Reported values of $739,320 fixed cost and $701,700 annual operation cost for the paper's assumed booth mix. Handoff: Possible Modification tests whether CTM survives autonomous vehicles and changed booth-type proportions.

Input: The base CTM assumes human driving, while autonomous vehicles may have different lane-recognition and turn behavior. Rhetorical job: Acknowledge the technology's growth, expose a condition-specific risk, and give a simple placement adaptation. Analytical job: Separate the autonomous route from complex curves by assigning it the leftmost straight path. Output: A qualitative left-lane modification rather than a new calibrated autonomous-flow model. Handoff: Section 6.2 then handles service-technology heterogeneity.

Input: Manual, automatic, and ETC booths have different service mechanisms and capacities. Rhetorical job: Show where CTM remains applicable, where nonstop ETC violates its assumptions, and how to reconfigure the left side. Analytical job: Compare typical service times, use approximately 2000 veh/h ETC capacity, allocate one ETC booth directly to one highway lane, and retain CTM elsewhere. Output: A hybrid layout: leftmost straight ETC flow plus the original controlled algorithm for remaining booths and lanes. Handoff: Sensitivity analysis next identifies which service and geometry parameters materially affect results.

Input: Hourly throughput depends on the service-time distribution parameters used by the simulation. Rhetorical job: Define sensitivity, display mean/variance perturbations, and reconcile the plot with the approximate inverse relation. Analytical job: Vary T and sigma, compare elasticities, and identify mean service time as the dominant throughput parameter. Output: A reported elasticity of -1 to mean service time and approximately 0 to variance in the plotted range. Handoff: The fixed-cost branch tests booth count, speed, and turning radius.

Input: Fixed cost is determined by geometry, booth count, speed, turning radius, and unit prices. Rhetorical job: Use a three-panel sensitivity figure to identify the main construction-cost lever and qualify less influential geometric parameters. Analytical job: Perturb B, v_m, and r around the stated initial tuple, compute elasticities, and connect booth additions to a cost-efficiency tradeoff. Output: Booth count is reported as the sensitive discrete parameter; speed limit and radius are comparatively insensitive. Handoff: Conclusion converts the selected CTM and sensitivity boundaries into one design specification.

Input: The paper has generated EM, CTM, and WAM, screened them by throughput, then analyzed CTM by safety, cost, modifications, and sensitivity. Rhetorical job: Turn the full chain into a concrete plaza specification and restate the worked B=8,L=3 values. Analytical job: Discard WAM, identify EM defects, retain CTM, summarize geometry, pattern, area, throughput, risk, fixed cost, and annual operation cost. Output: A CTM design with two tangent arcs, leading lines, near-even booth allocation, D=105.5 m, and the paper's reported performance/cost values. Handoff: Strengths and Weaknesses calibrates the recommendation before references and code.

Input: The selected CTM needs an explicit credibility and applicability assessment. Rhetorical job: List strengths first, then acknowledge trajectory, failure, arrival-process, and parameter-data weaknesses with partial remedies. Analytical job: Separate structural advantages from realism assumptions and missing empirical calibration. Output: A bounded conclusion: inspectable control and simulation benefits coexist with trajectory and data limitations. Handoff: References support context and the Appendix exposes the simulation algorithms.

Input: The main text reports simulation outputs whose event logic should be inspectable. Rhetorical job: Expose one implementation path for EM, CTM, WAM efficiency and EM/CTM PET simulation. Analytical job: Retain initialization, random service draws, queue ordering, recurrence branches, one-hour stops, and output vectors without treating code syntax as prose style. Output: A partial reproducibility bridge whose printed comparison operators and one runif call require source-level warning. Handoff: The artifact warning pass reconciles equations, claims, tables, and code before transaction closure.

assumptions.summary: Drivers obey rules, lane markings, control signals, and the prescribed booth-to-lane assignment.
Heavy traffic means every service booth continuously has at least one waiting vehicle.
Vehicle length, breakdowns, controller failure, weather, and downstream spillback are omitted.
Manual service time follows a source-described normal law N(15,4), interpreted in prose as variance 4 s^2.
A one-second same-lane release interval is taken as sufficient to avoid emergency braking.
Merge paths consist of two tangent uniform-radius arcs and use a common speed/acceleration convention.
Booth allocations are non-decreasing across downstream lanes and should differ as little as possible.
The main comparison uses two human-staffed booths merging into one lane for one simulated hour.
PET alone determines the asserted crash-probability proxy, with the same curve for EM and CTM.
The outer plaza boundary is symmetric and unit costs from the cited source transfer to the worked case.
Autonomous vehicles can be assigned to and remain in the leftmost straight lane.
One approximately 2,000 veh/h ETC booth can serve current demand and connect directly to one lane.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Notation defines B, L, D, d_B, d_L, T, t0, v_m, r, a, and service/control times with source units.
The controller alternates neighboring booths assigned to the same downstream lane and sets t0=1 s.
Worked geometry uses B=8, L=3 and reports D=105.5 m with three optimal assignments.
Throughput simulations use one-hour heavy-traffic runs and the paper reports N=1,000 runs per model.
Table 1 retains size, mean, standard deviation, and SEM for EM, CTM, and WAM.
Risk analysis uses PET, the visually checked p=exp(-PET)/100 proxy, and a claimed 4,000 simulations.
Table 2 prints 53.024 for EM and 61.416 for CTM per 100,000 vehicles.
Fixed-cost inputs include B=8, L=3, d_B=2.5 m, d_L=3.75 m, c_l=172.83, and three booth costs/proportions.
Annual inputs are c'_h=141,900, c'_e=4,200, c'_a=43,300 with proportions 4/8, 1/8, and 3/8.
Modification inputs include 15 s conventional service, 8 s automated service, 15 mph ETC speed, and about 2,000 veh/h ETC capacity.
Sensitivity baseline changes c_l to 172.84 and plots fixed cost against v_m, r, and B.
Appendix code uses R random draws but provides no seed, package/version record, or complete executable archive.

models.summary: MU-B-2017-70545-001: Classify free-route and predetermined-merge baselines and explain why heavy traffic creates unpredictable or simultaneous conflicts.
MU-B-2017-70545-002: Prevent two vehicles assigned to one lane from leaving neighboring booths within the chosen control interval.
MU-B-2017-70545-003: Relate the number of booths assigned to each downstream lane to interarrival time and total plaza throughput.
MU-B-2017-70545-004: Choose a non-decreasing booth-to-lane assignment and minimum two-arc merge length for given B and L.
MU-B-2017-70545-005: Allow a serviced vehicle to vacate the booth and wait for its controlled release so the following vehicle can begin service.
MU-B-2017-70545-006: Estimate EM throughput from two independent human-service streams plus PET-based conflict delay.
MU-B-2017-70545-007: Simulate service completions and enforce one-second mutual release spacing for two booths merging into one lane.
MU-B-2017-70545-008: Simulate WAM by allowing service clocks to advance independently of the controlled physical release clocks.
MU-B-2017-70545-009: Compare the 1,000-run throughput distributions, retain CTM as statistically near EM, and reject WAM on a small-benefit qualitative cost judgment.
MU-B-2017-70545-010: Compare EM and CTM conflict timing and translate PET into a per-100,000 risk proxy.
MU-B-2017-70545-011: Translate CTM geometry and the assumed booth mix into one-time land/construction cost and recurring annual operation cost.
MU-B-2017-70545-012: Protect the CTM from lane-marking and curvature-recognition failures by routing autonomous vehicles along the leftmost straight path.
MU-B-2017-70545-013: Separate nonstop ETC flow from stopped-service CTM flow and apply the original controller only to the residual subsystem.
MU-B-2017-70545-014: Perturb service and design parameters locally, identify dominant elasticities, and translate them into bounded cost-efficiency guidance.
MU-B-2017-70545-015: Select CTM after throughput screening, then bind geometry, operations, safety proxy, cost, modifications, sensitivity, and unresolved warnings to one recommendation.

verification.summary: All 26 physical pages and all substantive sections were read; Abstract/Summary and Introduction received the first deep passes.
Equation (1), release diagrams, actor labels, integration direction, and the t0 derivation were checked against focused crops.
Mapping, assignment, D objective, and B=8,L=3 geometry were reconciled across text and diagrams.
EM event equations and Figure 6 were traced into Appendix efficiency code.
CTM recurrences were reconciled with R's max updates and one-hour stopping rule.
WAM service/release clocks and the incomplete runif call were checked against the code listing.
All Table 1 values, the 0.0348 tail area, and the CTM-WAM 1.659 veh/h difference were recomputed.
The negative exponent in Equation (2) and the CTM PET floor were visually verified.
Table 2 row order was retained and tested against the claimed 13.66% reduction.
The literal area expression was evaluated and compared with the 1,824.93 m^2 one-direction claim.
The annual cost was recomputed; 701,700 requires c'_a p_a despite the printed expression.
Figure 10 was checked for the negative unit elasticity that the text layer/prose loses.
Figure 11 axes were checked as v_m, r, and B, then compared with the prose's D typo.
Appendix EM uses sd=4 while CTM/WAM and risk code use sd=2; the variance/standard-deviation inconsistency is retained.

results_trace.summary: For B=8,L=3, CTM reports D=105.5 m and three near-even booth-allocation patterns.
EM and CTM means are 477.830 and 477.422 veh/(h lane), with source z=1.813 and one-tail area 0.0348.
WAM exceeds CTM by 1.659 veh/(h lane) but is rejected because waiting-area cost is judged larger than the gain.
CTM imposes a one-second PET floor in the simulated event sequence.
The prose claims a 13.66% accident-rate reduction, while Table 2's printed row values imply the opposite direction.
The paper reports fixed cost of 739,320 USD for B=8,L=3.
The paper reports annual operation cost of 701,700 USD/year; the value is reproducible only under a reconstructed term.
Throughput elasticity to mean service time is -1 by formula and plot; dispersion sensitivity is approximately zero.
Fixed cost is locally most sensitive to B, with smaller v_m and r elasticities.
The conclusion selects CTM with two tangent arcs, leading lines, near-even allocation, and conditional modifications.

contributions.summary: The summary exposes a full baseline-to-controller-to-comparison-to-modification-to-sensitivity chain.
CTM converts a diagnosed simultaneous-release conflict into a simple operational timing rule.
Two-arc geometry ties controller operation to a concrete plaza footprint.
The mapping f and pattern vector make booth allocation an explicit combinatorial object.
WAM separates service completion from physical release and is evaluated rather than assumed superior.
A common run table and explicit hypothesis calculation make the model-screening decision inspectable.
PET supplies a safety-oriented comparison after throughput screening, even though calibration is missing.
Geometry, booth mix, and annual operation are brought into the same design ledger.
Modification sections state where CTM assumptions stop applying to autonomous and ETC flows.
Sensitivity plots connect parameter leverage to the final cost-efficiency discussion.

6.1 Autonomous-vehicle mixture: The base CTM assumes human driving, while autonomous vehicles may have different lane-recognition and turn behavior. -> A qualitative left-lane modification rather than a new calibrated autonomous-flow model. -> Section 6.2 then handles service-technology heterogeneity.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: The Summary previews baseline diagnosis, two candidate models, simulation, selection, modification, and sensitivity in judge-scannable order.
A common numeric table and explicit comparison make the screening decision inspectable, while the tail/equivalence interpretation needs correction.
The conclusion binds one worked geometry to throughput, risk, and cost, but credibility depends on carrying the source conflicts forward.

weaknesses.summary: Equation (1)'s actor labels, integration direction, and the t0>=t_res conclusion do not form a closed derivation.
t_i_k approximately T/i_k decreases with i_k, while the prose says it increases.
General geometric optimality is inferred from small worked configurations rather than proved for arbitrary B and L.
EM code uses rnorm(...,15,4), where 4 is sd, conflicting with prose variance 4 and CTM/WAM sd=2.
WAM defines both waiting-time labels as lane b and its appendix has runif(1,0,) without an upper bound.
0.0348 is a one-tail normal area; a conventional two-tail p-value is about 0.0696, and failure to reject does not prove equivalence.
Table 2 reverses the direction of the prose's 13.66% CTM reduction claim.
The area formula gives about 3,650.97 m^2 literally, while 1,824.93 m^2 requires an implicit one-half convention.
The printed annual formula contains undefined c'_2 and omits the term needed to reproduce 701,700.
The autonomous modification has no mixture, perception, capacity, safety, or cost recalculation, and its Sam citation is absent from References.
The ETC modification has no demand threshold and conflicts with the autonomous proposal for the leftmost lane.
Only local one-factor elasticities are shown; interactions and decision stability are untested.
Platform plurality is claimed as credibility without code parity, seeds, raw outputs, or external validation.
Appendix risk code omits the crash function, 4,000 repetitions, and Table 2 aggregation.

independent_extensions.summary: Re-derive the emergency-braking and control-time condition with consistent actors, bounds, units, and limiting cases.
Prove or computationally certify the assignment/geometry optimum over a stated B,L domain.
Use one documented service distribution and seed/replication ledger across EM, CTM, and WAM.
Use equivalence or noninferiority margins for the CTM-EM throughput decision and report confidence intervals.
Calibrate PET-to-crash risk on conflict/crash data and preserve exposure denominators.
Resolve Table 2 labels from executable output before using the 13.66% claim.
Normalize area and cost conventions, booth-type labels, currency year, and annual terms in a tested cost workbook.
Jointly allocate autonomous and ETC demand with lane capacity, compliance, safety, and fallback constraints.
Replace one-factor plots with global sensitivity, interactions, uncertainty propagation, and decision-switch thresholds.
Archive executable versions, dependencies, seeds, raw run tables, and cross-platform fixtures.

candidate_rule_impacts.action: retain condition, actor, quantity, operation, evidence class, result, boundary, and handoff in every toll-design claim
trace baseline defect through controller, geometry, candidate recurrence, comparison, safety, cost, modification, sensitivity, and authority recommendation
version every service, geometry, risk, booth-mix, and cost input with unit, source page, transformation, and downstream use
keep event times, assignment, geometry, throughput, PET risk, cost, elasticity, and decision outputs distinct
preflight signs, actors, dimensions, recurrences, code parameters, table labels, cost substitutions, and limiting cases
retain topology, axes, row order, exact values, negative signs, uncertainty boundaries, and accessible text alternatives
bound claims by local one-factor tests, missing seeds/calibration, table conflicts, and untested modifications
separate the Authority-facing recommendation from evidence and expose safety, driver, operator, land, and implementation burdens

unresolved_questions: Which actors and integration bounds make Equation (1) physically consistent?
Which Table 2 row labels match executable risk output?
Is service-time parameter 4 a variance or standard deviation in each model?
What global area convention produces 1,824.93 m^2 and 739,320 USD simultaneously?
How should autonomous and ETC demand share the leftmost lane?
Does CTM remain preferred after calibrated risk, arrival processes, breakdowns, and global uncertainty?
